name: Tube Screamer (TS808)
subtitle: Ibanez TS808 · 74 parts · Layers from a bare diode clipper to the full pedal

keyIdea.eli5: The diodes sit inside the op-amp's feedback loop, so they gently cap the boost instead of chopping the voltage. Tops round off softly, and some clean signal always rides along.
keyIdea.detail: A capacitor in the gain leg means bass barely gets boosted, and a sieve after the clipping trims the fizz: the famous mid hump. Step through Layers to watch the other 50-odd parts arrive.

summary: The real TS808 has 74 parts on ElectroSmash's schematic. Only 23 make the sound; the rest keep it quiet, protect it, buffer it and switch it. Layers builds it up one job at a time.

top.label: +9 V
top.eli5: Red is the + side of the battery.

bottom.label: 0 V (ground) · audio centered at 4.5 V
bottom.eli5: Blue is the battery's − side and ground.
bottom.detail: The op-amps and transistors need a middle to swing around, so a divider (R32, R33) makes a 4.5 V 'fake ground' inside the circuit. Grey wires on the board carry it.

groundNote.eli5: Ground here is the battery's − side (negative ground), the usual setup. The audio itself swings around the 4.5 V middle, not around ground.

notes: The original electrosmash.com page did not load from my fetchers; every ElectroSmash link points to the ElectroSmash archive copy, which I read in full.

honestyNote.eli5: A reasonable sketch of the sound, not a circuit solve. The board is schematic-faithful: real parts and values, my layout.

job.eli5: A transistor 'polite listener' gives the guitar an easy load and hands a strong copy on.

wire.eli5: The guitar, copied with more current behind it.

job.eli5: Op-amp boost with diodes that cap it. Where the diodes sit decides hard or soft clipping.

wire.eli5: Clipped mids, plus clean guitar riding underneath (from L2 on).

job.eli5: A sieve trims the fizz, a second op-amp runs the Tone knob, and the Level pot sets how loud.

wire.eli5: Smoothed overdrive at the level you picked.

job.eli5: A second polite listener drives the cable and the next pedal.

wire.eli5: The finished overdrive, to the amp.

job.eli5: The battery, a 4.5 V middle for the audio to swing around, tank caps and a guard diode.
A soft button flips a two-transistor memory that opens one JFET valve and closes the other: effect or clean.

parts.label: Input jack (stereo)
parts.term: stereo jack used as a power switch

job.eli5: Where the guitar plugs in. Its ring lug doubles as the battery switch.
job.detail: ElectroSmash: the stereo input jack switches the battery's minus side to ground when a guitar plug is in.

order.eli5: First thing the signal touches.

breaks.eli5: No signal in, and from L1 on no power either.

lugs.eli5: A stereo jack used as the power switch: plug in a mono cable and its sleeve bridges ring to sleeve, which turns the pedal on.
lugs.detail: ElectroSmash: the stereo input jack switches the battery's − terminal to ground when a guitar plug is in.
lugs.standard: Standard part: a ¼ inch stereo (TRS) jack, used this way in nearly every battery pedal.

lugs.name: tip
lugs.eli5: Your guitar's signal.

lugs.name: ring
lugs.eli5: The battery's − side, waiting for a plug to complete it.

lugs.name: sleeve
lugs.eli5: Ground and the cable shield.

job.eli5: Out to the amp.

order.eli5: End of the line.

breaks.eli5: No output.

parts.label: Input cap

job.eli5: A door that lets the guitar's wiggles in but blocks any steady push, both ways.
job.detail: ElectroSmash: it keeps the pedal's DC away from your pickups and trims the lowest hum.

order.eli5: First part on the board, right after the jack.

breaks.eli5: The buffer's resting voltage leaks onto your pickups; the input crackles and the buffer drifts.

parts.silentNote: The model has no pickup or cable to load, so you won't hear this one.

tune.higher: Bigger input cap: more deep bass gets into the pedal.
tune.lower: Smaller: the bass is cut before anything else happens.
tune.tooFar: Tiny and the pedal sounds like a telephone.

parts.label: Input series resistor

job.eli5: A small speed bump in front of the transistor that keeps radio buzz and sharp zaps out.
job.detail: My reading of its job: a base stopper, common in emitter followers. ElectroSmash doesn't single it out.

order.eli5: Between C1 and Q1's base.

breaks.eli5: Usually nothing you hear; the buffer is more likely to pick up radio or ring.

parts.silentNote: The model has no pickup or cable to load, so you won't hear this one.

job.eli5: A long leash that holds Q1's control pin at the 4.5 V middle, so the wave can swing both ways.
job.detail: ElectroSmash: the input impedance is about 446k, and this resistor sets almost all of it.

order.eli5: From Q1's base up to the 4.5 V middle.

breaks.eli5: Q1 has no resting point: it switches off and the signal nearly dies.

job.eli5: A polite listener: it copies the guitar's voltage, but with plenty of current behind it.
job.detail: An emitter follower has a gain of about 1. ElectroSmash: the 2SC1815 is cheap, high gain (beta about 350) and low noise.

order.eli5: First active part, before anything that would pull on the pickup.

breaks.eli5: Nothing gets past the input: silence.

lugs.eli5: A transistor is a valve with three legs: a tiny flow into the base controls a big flow from collector to emitter.
lugs.detail: The 2SC1815 is a small silicon NPN. Toshiba's datasheet gives the TO-92 lead order 1 emitter, 2 collector, 3 base (E C B), flat side facing you. Many NPNs (2N3904, BC547) use other orders, so check before you swap.
lugs.standard: Standard part: 2SC1815 (Toshiba). Common swaps: 2N5088/2N5089 or MPSA18, with a different pin order.

lugs.name: emitter (pin 1)
lugs.eli5: Out to C2 (and the dry switch at L6): the guitar's strong copy, across R3.

lugs.name: collector (pin 2)
lugs.eli5: Straight to +9 V.

lugs.name: base (pin 3)
lugs.eli5: In from R1, held at 4.5 V by R2.

job.eli5: The path to ground that lets Q1 follow: the copy of the guitar appears across it.

order.eli5: From Q1's emitter to ground.

breaks.eli5: Q1's emitter has nowhere to send current: no signal.

job.eli5: A door between stages: wiggles pass, steady voltages stay on their own side.
job.detail: ElectroSmash: 1 µF non-polarized, big enough to pass every guitar note. Before L5 it is the pedal's input cap.

order.eli5: Right before the op-amp's plus input.

breaks.eli5: The op-amp's 4.5 V middle and the guitar (or Q1) fight over the resting voltage: sputter or silence.

job.eli5: A plain wire on a resistor spot.
job.detail: ElectroSmash's schematic marks it RA with the note RA = 0 Ω. My reading: a spot kept for an input resistor in other versions.

order.eli5: Between C2 and the op-amp's plus input.

breaks.eli5: The path to the op-amp breaks: silence.

job.eli5: Ties the op-amp's plus input to the 4.5 V middle so it swings around half the battery.
job.detail: ElectroSmash: a single moderate 10k does the job here.

order.eli5: From the plus input (pin 3) up to the 4.5 V middle.

breaks.eli5: The plus input floats: hum, crackle, or an output stuck at one rail.

job.eli5: The engine: it boosts by the ratio of its feedback to its gain leg, and never drops below 1×.
job.detail: That 1× floor is why clean guitar always rides under a Tube Screamer's clipping. ElectroSmash: gain 12 to 118 before the diodes step in.

order.eli5: The heart of the clipping block.

breaks.eli5: No boost and no clipping: silence.

use.3: The guitar in, resting at 4.5 V (R5).
use.2: Feedback point: R4 + C3 to ground, R6 + Drive back from pin 1, and from L2 the diodes and C4.
use.1: Clipping out, to R7 (or to C7 before L3).
use.5: Op-amp B: the tone stage (from L3).

chip.note: ElectroSmash's schematic says JRC4558 (labeled JNR4558); TI's RC4558 has the same pinout.

job.eli5: The minimum boost: even with Drive at zero, this sets about 12× against the 4.7k gain leg.

order.eli5: In the feedback, in series with the Drive pot.

breaks.eli5: With no feedback path the op-amp boosts as hard as it can: everything slams into the diodes or the rails.

tune.higher: Bigger minimum-feedback resistor: more gain even with Drive at zero.
tune.lower: Smaller: Drive at zero gets closer to a clean boost.
tune.tooFar: Very big and the bottom of the Drive knob is already heavy; zero and the bottom is almost clean (gain 1).

parts.label: Drive pot
parts.term: pot in the feedback path (log taper)

job.eli5: The Drive knob: more feedback resistance, more boost, the diodes get pushed harder.
job.detail: ElectroSmash: 500k log. The wiper is tied to one end, so it works as a variable resistor.

order.eli5: In the feedback, from the op-amp's output back toward its minus input.

breaks.eli5: Drive stuck wherever it lands.

tune.higher: Bigger Drive pot: more gain at full turn.
tune.lower: Smaller: the Drive knob tops out lower, more like a boost.
tune.tooFar: Very big and the top of the knob gets noisy and squeally.

lugs.eli5: A pot is a resistor with a slider: two end lugs and a wiper in the middle that rides along the track.
lugs.detail: Use all three lugs and it is a voltage divider (a volume knob). Use one end and the wiper and it is a variable resistor (a faucet).
lugs.standard: Standard part: a potentiometer (A = log taper for volume, B = linear).

lugs.name: end 1
lugs.eli5: One end of the resistive track.

lugs.name: wiper
lugs.eli5: The middle lug rides along the track as you turn: here it is tied to end 3, so it is a faucet in the feedback.

lugs.name: end 3
lugs.eli5: The other end of the track.

job.eli5: Two one-way valves facing opposite ways: when the swing gets too big, one opens and caps it.
job.detail: On L0 and L1 they hang from the signal to ground and pin the voltage at about 0.6 V (hard clipping). From L2 they sit in the op-amp's feedback, so they cap the gain instead and the tops come out round. ElectroSmash: D1 clips the top half, D2 the bottom.

order.eli5: Where they sit is the whole difference between hard and soft clipping.
order.detail: To ground: the voltage itself gets chopped. In the feedback: the gain drops toward 1× once a diode turns on.

breaks.eli5: No clipping: a clean, loud boost (from L1 on), or a plain cable (L0).

choices.label: silicon (MA150)
choices.eli5: The stock pair: clips at about 0.6 V, the classic smooth Tube Screamer.

choices.label: germanium
choices.eli5: Lower threshold, softer knee: earlier, mellower, quieter clipping (the Distortion+ uses 1N270s).

choices.label: red LEDs
choices.eli5: Higher threshold: louder, more open, more amp-like.

choices.label: none
choices.eli5: No diodes: just the op-amp's gain until it slams into the rails. Loud and raw.

tune.tooFar: Mismatched diodes clip unevenly (that can be a nice asymmetric flavor). LEDs need more voltage swing than a 9 V op-amp likes.

job.eli5: A shortcut for very fast wiggles across the diodes, so the fizz gets less boost.
job.detail: ElectroSmash: it softens the clipped corners, most when Drive is up.

order.eli5: Across the diodes, inside the feedback.

breaks.eli5: Fizzier, more brittle highs.

tune.higher: Bigger feedback cap: the clipping gets darker and smoother.
tune.tooFar: Too big and it goes woolly; leave it out and the fizz gets harsh.

job.eli5: The bottom half of the boost ratio: smaller means more boost.

order.eli5: From the op-amp's minus input toward ground, through C3.

breaks.eli5: The ratio falls apart: no boost.

tune.higher: Bigger gain-leg resistor: less gain and a lower mid hump corner, so it gets smoother and cleaner.
tune.lower: Smaller: more gain, and the hump moves up: tight, nasal and loud.
tune.tooFar: Very small and the op-amp squeals or runs out of headroom; very big and the drive barely bites.

job.eli5: A door that keeps bass out of the gain leg, so bass gets almost no boost and the mids get it all.
job.detail: ElectroSmash: with 4.7k it sets about 720 Hz. The MXR Distortion+ uses the same 4.7k + 47 nF.

order.eli5: In series with R4, to ground.

breaks.eli5: No path to ground: the boost collapses to 1×.

tune.higher: Bigger gain-leg cap: bass gets clipped too, so it gets fat and less 'Tube Screamer'.
tune.lower: Smaller: only the mids and highs clip, tight and nasal.
tune.tooFar: Large (1 µF) and it loses the famous mid hump; tiny and it sounds like a buzzing radio.

job.eli5: Half of a sieve with C5: lows pass, the fizz above about 723 Hz gets held back.
job.detail: ElectroSmash: 1k + 0.22 µF = 723 Hz, first order (6 dB per octave).

order.eli5: Right after the clipping amp.

breaks.eli5: The signal can't reach the tone stage: silence.

tune.higher: Bigger tone resistor: the treble corner drops, so it gets darker.
tune.tooFar: Very big and the Tone knob can't rescue the highs.

job.eli5: The other half of the sieve: it hands the highs to ground.

order.eli5: From after R7 to ground.

breaks.eli5: Harsh, fizzy top end.

tune.tooFar: Very big and it's muffled; tiny and the fizz pours through.

job.eli5: Ties the tone op-amp's plus input to the 4.5 V middle.

order.eli5: From pin 5 up to the 4.5 V middle.

breaks.eli5: Pin 5 floats: hum, crackle, or a stuck output.

job.eli5: The second op-amp in the same chip runs the tone control, so the knob can hand treble back as well as take it.
job.detail: ElectroSmash: the tone network sits between its two inputs.

order.eli5: After the passive sieve.

breaks.eli5: No path through the tone stage: silence.

use.5: The sieved signal from R7 + C5, resting at 4.5 V (R9), plus one end of the Tone pot.
use.6: The Tone pot's other end and the R11 feedback.

chip.note: The second op-amp in the same chip.

job.eli5: The Tone knob: toward treble it hands back highs, toward bass it takes more away.
job.detail: ElectroSmash: 20k with a G (S) taper, so the middle of the sweep gets the finest control.

order.eli5: Strung between the tone op-amp's two inputs, with R8 + C6 on the wiper.

breaks.eli5: Tone stuck in one place.

tune.higher: Bigger tone pot: a wider sweep, darker at one end.
tune.tooFar: Far off and one end of the knob does nothing useful.
tune.real: On the real board the active tone stage also boosts; the sketch only moves the treble corner.

lugs.eli5: A pot is a resistor with a slider: two end lugs and a wiper in the middle that rides along the track.
lugs.detail: Use all three lugs and it is a voltage divider (a volume knob). Use one end and the wiper and it is a variable resistor (a faucet).
lugs.standard: Standard part: a potentiometer (A = log taper for volume, B = linear).

lugs.name: end 1
lugs.eli5: One end of the resistive track.

lugs.name: wiper
lugs.eli5: The middle lug rides along the track as you turn: it drains treble to ground through C6 and R8.

lugs.name: end 3
lugs.eli5: The other end of the track.

job.eli5: With C6, a little drain for treble on the Tone pot's wiper.
job.detail: ElectroSmash: 220 Ω + 0.22 µF, about 3.2 kHz.

order.eli5: From C6 to ground.

breaks.eli5: The Tone knob stops doing much.

job.eli5: The other half of the treble drain on the Tone wiper.

order.eli5: Between the Tone pot's wiper and R8.

breaks.eli5: The Tone knob stops doing much.

job.eli5: Closes the tone op-amp's loop, so it works at about 1×.
job.detail: ElectroSmash's drawing labels both 1k resistors around the tone op-amp R11; I call this one R11 (tone feedback).

order.eli5: From the tone op-amp's output (pin 7) back to its minus input (pin 6).

breaks.eli5: No feedback: the tone op-amp slams into its rails.

parts.label: Output coupling cap

job.eli5: A door that passes the overdrive but keeps the op-amp's 4.5 V middle away from the Level pot.

order.eli5: After the tone op-amp (before L3: after the clipping amp).

breaks.eli5: Steady push on the Level pot: scratchy knob and a thump when you switch.

parts.silentNote: The steady push makes no sound, so the model can't show it.

job.eli5: A small bump between the tone stage and the Level pot.
job.detail: On L1 it also feeds the diodes to ground, like the 10k in front of the MXR Distortion+'s diodes. ElectroSmash labels it R11 too.

order.eli5: Between C7 and the top of the Level pot.

breaks.eli5: No signal reaches the Level pot: silence.

job.eli5: The volume slider: the wiper picks how much of the overdrive goes on.
job.detail: ElectroSmash: a 100k pot that bleeds part of the signal to ground.

order.eli5: Last stop before the output buffer (or the jack, before L5).

breaks.eli5: Full blast always.

tune.higher: Bigger: a softer load, a touch brighter.
tune.lower: Smaller: it loads the tone stage a little.
tune.tooFar: Very small and it drags the output down.
tune.real: This sketch does not model it.

lugs.eli5: A pot is a resistor with a slider: two end lugs and a wiper in the middle that rides along the track.
lugs.detail: Use all three lugs and it is a voltage divider (a volume knob). Use one end and the wiper and it is a variable resistor (a faucet).
lugs.standard: Standard part: a potentiometer (A = log taper for volume, B = linear).

lugs.name: end 1
lugs.eli5: One end of the resistive track.

lugs.name: wiper
lugs.eli5: The middle lug rides along the track as you turn: it taps off as much overdrive as you want.

lugs.name: end 3
lugs.eli5: The other end of the track.

parts.label: Output buffer input cap

job.eli5: A door into the output buffer.
job.detail: ElectroSmash: with C11 it keeps the JFET switches' DC conditions separate from the rest of the circuit.

order.eli5: Between the switches (or the Level pot) and Q3's base.

breaks.eli5: Q3 loses its resting point to whatever feeds it: weak, uneven output.

parts.silentNote: The model has no pickup or cable to load, so you won't hear this one.

job.eli5: Holds Q3's control pin at the 4.5 V middle.
job.detail: ElectroSmash: the output buffer is biased from the 4.5 V source through 510k.

order.eli5: From Q3's base up to the 4.5 V middle.

breaks.eli5: Q3 switches off: almost no output.

job.eli5: A second polite listener, so the cable and the next pedal can't drag the sound down.
job.detail: ElectroSmash: unity gain, output impedance about 1.2k.

order.eli5: Last active part.

breaks.eli5: Nothing reaches the output jack: silence.

lugs.eli5: A transistor is a valve with three legs: a tiny flow into the base controls a big flow from collector to emitter.
lugs.detail: The 2SC1815 is a small silicon NPN. Toshiba's datasheet gives the TO-92 lead order 1 emitter, 2 collector, 3 base (E C B), flat side facing you. Many NPNs (2N3904, BC547) use other orders, so check before you swap.
lugs.standard: Standard part: 2SC1815 (Toshiba). Common swaps: 2N5088/2N5089 or MPSA18, with a different pin order.

lugs.name: emitter (pin 1)
lugs.eli5: Out through RB and C9 to the jack, across R13.

lugs.name: collector (pin 2)
lugs.eli5: Straight to +9 V.

lugs.name: base (pin 3)
lugs.eli5: In from C8, held at 4.5 V by R12.

job.eli5: The path to ground that lets Q3 follow.

order.eli5: From Q3's emitter to ground.

breaks.eli5: No output.

parts.label: Output series resistor

job.eli5: A small bump that keeps the output buffer calm into long cables.
job.detail: ElectroSmash: it slightly limits drive and forms an inaudible divider with RC. The TS9 uses 470 Ω here.

order.eli5: Between Q3's emitter and C9.

breaks.eli5: A slightly hotter, touchier output; often no audible change.

parts.silentNote: The model has no pickup or cable to load, so you won't hear this one.

tune.higher: Bigger output resistor (the TS9 uses 470 Ω): a hair less drive into the cable.
tune.tooFar: Large values start to eat level and highs into a long cable.
tune.real: On a real rig the TS808/TS9 output difference is subtle; the sketch nudges level only.

parts.label: Output cap

job.eli5: A door that passes the sound but keeps the buffer's resting voltage off your amp.

order.eli5: Between RB and the output jack.

breaks.eli5: Steady push on the output: a thump at the amp and scratchy switching.

parts.silentNote: The steady push makes no sound, so the model can't show it.

parts.label: Output pulldown

job.eli5: A slow leak to ground at the jack, so the output cap has nothing stored up to pop.
job.detail: ElectroSmash: it shunts the output after C9. The TS9 uses 100k here.

order.eli5: From the output jack to ground.

breaks.eli5: A pop when you plug in or switch.

parts.silentNote: The model has no pickup or cable to load, so you won't hear this one.

tune.higher: Bigger pulldown (the TS9 uses 100k): a lighter load, a little hotter output.
tune.lower: Smaller: it loads the output more.
tune.tooFar: Very small and it eats level; leave it out and the output cap pops.

job.eli5: The fuel tank. The DC jack lets a wall supply take over from the battery.

order.eli5: Feeds every rail.

breaks.eli5: No power: silence from L1 on.

job.eli5: The top half of a two-step ladder that splits 9 V into a 4.5 V middle.
job.detail: ElectroSmash: R32 and R33 make the 4.5 V bias for the stages.

order.eli5: From +9 V to the 4.5 V node.

breaks.eli5: No middle voltage: every stage rests at 0 V, so half of each wave gets cut off.

job.eli5: The bottom half of the ladder, down to ground.

order.eli5: From the 4.5 V node to ground.

breaks.eli5: The middle floats up to 9 V: every stage jams against its top rail.

parts.label: 4.5 V tank cap

job.eli5: A tank on the 4.5 V middle, so every stage sees a calm, steady middle.
job.detail: ElectroSmash: 47 µF to ground removes ripple. Without it the stages talk to each other through the shared middle.

order.eli5: Across R32, from the 4.5 V node to ground.

breaks.eli5: Hiss and hum ride in on the middle; with high gain the pedal can squeal or motorboat.

parts.silentNote: Power hygiene isn't modeled (the sketch has no hum, ripple or battery sag), so you won't hear this.

parts.label: 9 V tank cap

job.eli5: A tank on the 9 V line that smooths out supply ripple and long-cable dips.
job.detail: ElectroSmash: 100 µF to ground removes ripple from the supply.

order.eli5: From +9 V to ground, right at the power input.

breaks.eli5: Wall-wart hum and a fizzy, sagging edge when the battery is weak.

parts.silentNote: Power hygiene isn't modeled (the sketch has no hum, ripple or battery sag), so you won't hear this.

parts.label: Reverse-polarity diode

job.eli5: A guard: plug in a supply backwards and it shorts the wrong way round instead of the chip.
job.detail: ElectroSmash: D8 protects the pedal against reverse polarity. It sits across the supply, so a backwards supply goes through it, not the circuit.

order.eli5: Across the supply, pointing so it only conducts when the polarity is wrong.

breaks.eli5: Nothing changes until someone plugs in the wrong supply. Then the 4558 can die.

parts.silentNote: Power hygiene isn't modeled (the sketch has no hum, ripple or battery sag), so you won't hear this.

parts.label: Dry path cap

job.eli5: A door between the input buffer and the bypass switch.
job.detail: ElectroSmash's drawing names two caps C11. This one (0.1 µF) keeps the JFET's DC conditions apart from Q1.

order.eli5: From Q1's emitter to switch B.

breaks.eli5: When bypassed, the switch's 4.5 V resting point fights Q1's: weak or crackly bypass.

parts.silentNote: The model doesn't simulate the switching circuit, so pulling this changes nothing you hear. On the real board, see 'If pulled'.

parts.label: Switch B bias

job.eli5: Holds switch B's input at the 4.5 V middle.
job.detail: ElectroSmash: the JFETs' drains and sources rest at 4.5 V through 510k (R17, R18, R12).

order.eli5: From switch B's input up to 4.5 V.

breaks.eli5: Switch B drifts: bypass gets crackly or won't fully open.

parts.silentNote: The model doesn't simulate the switching circuit, so pulling this changes nothing you hear. On the real board, see 'If pulled'.

job.eli5: A valve in the effect path: wide open when the pedal is on, shut when it's off.
job.detail: ElectroSmash: on when its gate sits at 0 V against its channel, off when the gate is pulled down near 0 V absolute so diode D3 forward-biases.

order.eli5: Between the Level pot and the output buffer.

breaks.eli5: The effect never reaches the output: you only hear the bypass path.

lugs.eli5: A JFET switch is a valve that is wide open when its gate matches the channel, and shut when the gate is pulled well below it.
lugs.detail: The 2SK44 is an N-channel JFET in TO-92. Lead order S G D comes from a pinout listing (pinout.net), not a maker datasheet I could open, so check yours with a meter. Drain and source are interchangeable in a switch like this.
lugs.standard: Obsolete Sanyo/Toshiba part. Clones use 2N5457, J201 or 2SK30A, each with its own pin order.

lugs.name: gate (pin 2)

lugs.name: drain (pin 3)
lugs.eli5: From the Level pot's wiper: the effect.

order.eli5: Between the dry cap C11 and the output buffer.

lugs.standard: Obsolete Sanyo/Toshiba part. Clones use 2N5457, J201 or 2SK30A, each with its own pin order.

lugs.name: gate (pin 2)

job.eli5: Holds the two switches' shared output at 4.5 V.

rungs.label: L0
rungs.title: Bare diode clipper

why.eli5: Two diodes from the guitar wire to ground already distort: any swing past about 0.6 V gets chopped flat. But it's quiet, thin and fizzy, because nothing boosts the guitar and the diodes drag on the pickup.
why.detail: No battery, no gain. The diodes only touch the loudest peaks of a hot pickup, so most notes come through clean and small, and the loudest ones clip hard. They also load the pickup, which costs level and sparkle. Everything after this rung is about fixing those limits.

rungs.hearNote: Quiet, thin, with fizzy hard clipping only on the loudest picks. No knobs yet.

pedals.name: No production pedal
pedals.note: No real pedal stops this early: it can't boost, so it is a lesson, not a product. Try it live in Falstad.

link.label: Falstad: diode clipper you can poke

rungs.label: L1
rungs.title: Op-amp boost + diodes to ground

why.eli5: An op-amp boosts the guitar up to 118 times before the diodes, so every note clips, not just the loud ones. Hard and harsh, but loud and with a Drive knob.
why.detail: This is the MXR Distortion+ and DOD 250 recipe: one op-amp with 4.7k + 47 nF to ground in its gain leg, then diodes to ground. Those pedals put the gain pot in the gain leg; this ladder keeps the TS layout and turns the Drive pot in the feedback. The op-amp needs a middle to swing around, so the 4.5 V divider (R32, R33) arrives here, not at L4.

rungs.hearNote: Loud, buzzy, square-ish clipping. Drive and Level work; there's no Tone knob yet.

pedals.name: MXR Distortion+
pedals.note: One 741 op-amp, 4.7k + 47 nF gain leg, germanium diodes to ground, a Level pot. Almost exactly this rung.

pedals.name: DOD 250 Overdrive Preamp
pedals.note: Same idea: one 741, the gain pot in the gain leg, a diode pair to ground after a resistor.

rungs.label: L2
rungs.title: Diodes into the feedback: soft clipping

why.eli5: Move the same two diodes into the op-amp's feedback and the tops round off instead of chopping. Smooth, and the clean guitar always rides along underneath.
why.detail: In the feedback, a diode that turns on lowers the gain toward 1× rather than pinning the voltage. The op-amp never drops below 1×, so some clean signal always gets through: that blend is half the Tube Screamer feel. Bass sees almost no boost (the 47 nF gain-leg door), so it stays clean while the mids clip: the start of the mid hump. C4 (51 pF) takes the edge off the fizz.

rungs.hearNote: Smoother and less buzzy than L1, with clean bass under the clipped mids.

pedals.name: Boss OD-1 OverDrive
pedals.note: The first pedal with diodes in the feedback loop (1977). It has Level and Drive, no Tone knob.

link.label: Aion FX: Corona (Boss OD-1 clone) build doc, with schematic

rungs.label: L3
rungs.title: Tone + volume stage

why.eli5: A sieve trims the fizz after the clipping, and the second op-amp in the same chip runs a Tone knob. Now it's the Tube Screamer sound, mid hump and all.
why.detail: ElectroSmash: R7 + C5 roll off above 723 Hz, the Tone pot sits between op-amp B's two inputs with R8 + C6 on its wiper, and the 100k Level pot sets the volume. Cutting bass before the clipper and treble after it is what makes the hump.

rungs.hearNote: The Tone knob arrives: warm and round to bright and cutting.

pedals.name: No pedal stops exactly here
pedals.note: This is the TS808's whole sound path. Every production TS also has the power and buffer parts from the next rungs.

rungs.label: L4
rungs.title: Tank caps + guard diode

why.eli5: Why all these caps to 4.5 V? Tanks on the 9 V line and on the 4.5 V middle keep the supply calm, and a guard diode survives a backwards plug. You won't hear a difference here, but a real board without them hums, hisses or squeals.
why.detail: ElectroSmash: C17 (100 µF) and C16 (47 µF) remove ripple; D8 protects against reverse polarity. Without C16, every stage shares a wobbly middle, and with high gain that shared wobble can feed back into a squeal or a 'motorboat' putt.

rungs.hearNote: Explain-only: the model has no hum, ripple or battery sag, so nothing changes.

pedals.name: Every pedal from here on
pedals.note: No famous pedal is known for its tank caps. The MXR Distortion+ already filters its own reference with a cap.

rungs.label: L5
rungs.title: Input + output buffers

why.eli5: Two transistor 'polite listeners' sit at the ends: the guitar sees an easy load, and long cables after the pedal can't dull the highs. Tone suck is the problem they fix.
why.detail: Q1 and Q3 are emitter followers: gain about 1, input about 446k, output about 1.2k (ElectroSmash). In a behavioral model with no pickup and no cable there is nothing to load, so the sound stays the same. This is also exactly ElectroSmash's true-bypass TS808: 38 parts plus a 3PDT.

rungs.hearNote: Explain-only: the sketch has no pickup or cable to load. On a real rig, they keep the sparkle with long cables.

pedals.name: True-bypass TS808 clones
pedals.note: ElectroSmash's true-bypass TS808 keeps both buffers, swaps the JFET switching for a 3PDT, and lists 38 board parts.

rungs.label: L6
rungs.title: JFET bypass + soft button: the full TS808

why.eli5: A soft button flips a two-transistor memory, which opens one JFET valve and shuts the other, and lights the LED. Click-free switching, and the buffers stay on even when bypassed.
why.detail: ElectroSmash: Q5 and Q6 form a flip-flop that a momentary switch toggles through C13, C14 and C15; the 1M resistors and 47 nF caps slow the JFETs so they don't pop; D7 and R31 keep the LED from upsetting the toggle; mismatched speed-up caps make it always wake up bypassed. Ibanez did this because momentary switches are cheaper and more reliable than hand-wired 3PDTs, not for tone.

rungs.hearNote: Effect-on sounds the same as L5. The difference is bypass: here 'off' still runs through both buffers (try the footswitch). Pops and LED draw aren't modeled.

pedals.name: Ibanez TS808 Tube Screamer
pedals.note: The real thing: 74 parts on ElectroSmash's schematic, counting the pots, the LED and the switch, but not the jacks or battery.

rungs.label: TS9
rungs.title: TS9: the output resistors

why.eli5: The TS9 is almost the same pedal: the main circuit change is two output resistors, 470 Ω instead of 100 Ω and 100k instead of 10k.
why.detail: Singlecoil's 808 mod: swap R55 (470 Ω) for 100 Ω and R58 (100k) for 10k. The difference is subtle: a touch brighter and hotter into some amps. Chips and caps varied by year, which also gets credit.

rungs.hearNote: A small nudge in the model: a little louder and brighter. On a real rig, many people can't hear it.

pedals.name: Ibanez TS9
pedals.note: Same core as the TS808, different output resistors.

link.label: Singlecoil: converting a TS9 into an 808 (PDF)

rungs.label: Klon
rungs.title: What boutique pedals add next: Klon Centaur

why.eli5: Boutique overdrives add things the TS doesn't have: the Klon Centaur blends clean signal back in through feedforward paths and a summing op-amp, and a charge pump turns 9 V into about 18 V for more headroom.
why.detail: ElectroSmash: a TC1044 charge pump makes +18 V and −9 V from the battery; two 1N34A germanium diodes clip to ground (hard clipping, like the Distortion+); feedforward networks and a summing op-amp mix the clean and clipped paths. Not drawn here: it is a different circuit, not one more layer on this board.

rungs.hearNote: Explain-only: a different circuit, read the analysis.

pedals.name: Klon Centaur
pedals.note: Clean blend (feedforward + summing op-amp), 18 V charge pump, germanium diodes to ground.
